--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Non-spatial mark-recapture for
estimating population size' slide-number: true echo: true lang: en --- ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 140%;"}
**Non-spatial mark-recapture for
estimating population size**
::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} WILD(FISH) 8390
Inference for Models of Fish and Wildlife Population Dynamics
:::
# Overview {visibility="hidden"} ## Mark-recapture overview Until now, we've focused on models for data on aggregated quantities like abundance and occupancy.
Now we will talk about data on uniquely identifiable individuals.
::: {.fragment} This is nice because all individuals are different, and we're often interested in these differences, even when our primary goal is inference on population-level parameters like abundance and density. ::: ## Closed populations ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} For this lecture, we will assume population closure: - No births or deaths during the time of sampling (demographic closure) - No permanent immigration or emigration (geographic closure) ::: {.fragment} There are several other assumptions that depend on the specific model being employed, including: - No misidentification - No band/tag loss - etc... ::: ::: {.fragment} Later, we will relax the closure assumption so that we can study survival, recruitment, and movement. ::: ::: ## Mark-recapture overview ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} The simplest estimator of abundance is $$ \hat{N} = \frac{n}{\hat{p}} $$ where $n$ is the number of individuals detected, $p$ is detection probability, and $E(n)=Np$.
In distance sampling, we modeled detection probability as a function of distance, and we replaced $p$ with average detection probability.
::: {.fragment} For the simplest mark-recapture problems, $p$ is a constant (scalar) and we estimate it by trapping on multiple occasions and marking and recapturing as we go. ::: ::: ## Classical approaches ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} Lincoln-Peterson - $J=2$ occasions - Data are: * $n_1$ -- number of individuals captured on first occasion * $n_2$ -- number of individuals captured on second occasion * $m_2$ -- number of recaptures Estimator is $\hat{N} = n_1n_2/m_2$ ::: {.fragment} Closed population models - Usually better to have $J>2$ occasions - Allows for assessment of behavioral effects, individual heterogeneity, etc... ::: ::: ## Mark-recapture data ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Mark-recapture data are often called "capture histories." Here's an example with $n=6$ animals captured on $J=3$ occasions. ::: {style='font-size: 60%;'}
Individual | 1 | 2 | 3 ------ | -- | -- | -- 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 3 | 0 | 1 | 0 4 | 0 | 1 | 1 5 | 1 | 0 | 0 6 | 0 | 0 | 1
::: How do we estimate $p$ (and $N$) from these data? :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {style='font-size: 65%;'} Conceptually... - If $p\approx 1$, most individuals would be captured on all 3 occasions, and few would go undetected - If $p\approx 0$, few individuals would be captured more than once, and many would go undetected ::: ::: ## [Closed population model (if we knew *N*)]{style="font-size: 85%;"} ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} **State model** There isn't one! $N$ is often treated as a constant, although we sometimes put a Poisson or binomial prior on it. ::: {.fragment} **Observation model** (supposing $N$ was known) $$ y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p) \;\; \mathrm{for}\, i=1,\dots,N $$ - $N$ -- Population size - $y_{ij}$ -- Capture histories, indicating if individual $i$ was captured on occasion $j$ - $p$ -- Capture probability ::: ::: {.fragment} The problem with this formulation is that we don't observe the "all zero" encounter histories (and thus we don't know $N$). As a result, the Bernoulli assumption isn't valid, and we need to develop a model that describes how many individuals we failed to capture. ::: ::: ## Closed population estimation options ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} **Conditional likelihood** - Estimate $p$, and then estimate $N$ as a derived quantity. - Most software is based on the work by Huggins, which allows for continuous covariates. ::: {.fragment} **Joint likelihood** - Estimate $N$ and $p$ jointly ::: ::: {.fragment} **Data augmentation** - Tack on many "all zero" encounter histories and estimate how many of them actually occurred - Usually, but not necessarily, used in Bayesian inference ::: ::: ## Joint likelihood ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} The joint likelihood is based on the multinomial distribution, with the "all-zero" encounter history being unobserved. $$ \{f_1, \dots, f_{K+1}\} \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_{K+1}) \;\; $$ where $\{f_1, \dots, f_K\}$ are the frequencies of the observable capture histories. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Here's an example with $J=3$ capture occasions.
:::
::: {style='font-size: 50%;'} Capture history | Multinomial cell probability ----------------- | ----------------------------- 100 | $\pi_1=p_1(1-p_2)(1-p_3)$ 010 | $\pi_2=(1-p_1)p_2(1-p_3)$ 001 | $\pi_3=(1-p_1)(1-p_2)p_3$ 110 | $\pi_4=p_1p_2(1-p_3)$ 101 | $\pi_5=p_1(1-p_2)p_3$ 011 | $\pi_6=(1-p_1)p_2p_3$ 111 | $\pi_7 = p_1p_2p_3$ 000 | $\pi_0 = \prod_j 1-p_j$ :::
::: ## Model variations ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} More important than the estimation approach, is identification of the sources of variation in capture probability ($p$). Otis et al. (1978) identified several model variations: - $M_0$ -- $p$ is constant - $M_t$ -- unique $p$ for each capture occasion - $M_b$ -- behavioral response with $p$ different than recapture probability $c$ - $M_h$ -- individual heterogeneity in $p$ - Finite mixture models - Continuous mixture models (not available in RMark) These can be combined, but beware of identifiability issues. See Otis et al. (1978) for details. Later we'll talk about "individual covariate" models. ::: ## Software options ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Program MARK - Has the most model types - Written for Windows, but can be executed on other platforms R package 'RMark' - Function `mark` runs MARK from R. R package 'marked' - Includes CJS and JS models R package 'mra' - Includes closed-population, CJS, and JS models R package 'Rcapture' - Includes closed-population R package 'unmarked' - Likelihood-based data augmentation with \inr{occu} R package 'secr' - Designed for spatially explicit models, but see \inr{closedN} ::: # Simulation ## Model *M~0~* ::: {style='font-size: 75%;'} Parameters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} N <- 100 p <- 0.2 ``` ::: All capture histories (for captured and uncaptured individuals) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} J <- 4 ## Occasions y.all <- matrix(NA, N, J) for(i in 1:N) { y.all[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p) } ``` ::: Observed capture histories (data) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} captured <- rowSums(y.all)>0 (n <- sum(captured)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 54 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y <- y.all[captured,] y[1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 0 1 0 0 [2,] 1 0 0 0 [3,] 0 0 1 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Summary stats Capture history frequencies ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} histories <- apply(y, 1, paste, collapse="") sort(table(histories)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` histories 0011 0101 1100 1010 1101 0110 1001 0001 0010 0100 1000 1 1 1 2 2 4 4 7 10 10 12 ``` ::: :::
Detection frequencies ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.tilde <- rowSums(y) sort(table(y.tilde)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` y.tilde 3 2 1 2 13 39 ``` ::: ::: ## Model *M~t~* -- Temporal variation ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Capture probability for each occasion ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p.t <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.4) ``` ::: All capture histories (for captured and uncaptured individuals) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.all.Mt <- matrix(NA, N, J) for(i in 1:N) { y.all.Mt[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p.t) } ``` ::: Observed capture histories (data) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} captured.Mt <- rowSums(y.all.Mt)>0 n.Mt <- sum(captured.Mt) y.Mt <- y.all.Mt[captured.Mt,] y.Mt[1:3,] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 1 0 1 0 [2,] 1 1 1 0 [3,] 1 0 0 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} colSums(y.Mt) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 28 53 22 38 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Model *M~b~* -- Behavioral response ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Capture probability for each occasion ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p.b <- 0.3 c <- 0.5 ## Trap happy ``` ::: All capture histories (for captured and uncaptured individuals) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.all.Mb <- matrix(NA, N, J) prevcap <- matrix(FALSE, N, J) for(i in 1:N) { y.all.Mb[i,1] <- rbinom(1, 1, p.b) for(j in 2:J) { prevcap[i,j] <- any(y.all.Mb[i,1:(j-1)]>0) prob <- ifelse(prevcap[i,j], c, p.b) y.all.Mb[i,j] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob) } } ``` ::: Observed capture histories (data) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} captured.Mb <- rowSums(y.all.Mb)>0 n.Mb <- sum(captured.Mb) y.Mb <- y.all.Mb[captured.Mb,] ## prevcap[1:3,] ``` ::: ::: ## Model *M~h~* -- Finite mixture ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} There are many flavors of $M_h$. This one assumes there are two (unknown) groups of individuals with different capture probs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mixture.prob <- 0.6 group <- rbinom(N, 1, mixture.prob) ## Two groups p.Mh.mix <- ifelse(group==0, 0.2, 0.7) ## Two-point mixture ``` ::: All capture histories (for captured and uncaptured individuals) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.all.Mh.mix <- matrix(NA, N, J) for(i in 1:N) { y.all.Mh.mix[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p.Mh.mix[i]) } ``` ::: Observed capture histories (data) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} captured.Mh.mix <- rowSums(y.all.Mh.mix)>0 n.Mh.mix <- sum(captured.Mh.mix) y.Mh.mix <- y.all.Mh.mix[captured.Mh.mix,] ``` ::: ::: ## Model *M~h~* -- Individual heterogeneity ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Here's another flavor of $M_h$: logit-normal distribution for $p$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} logit.p.bar <- -1 ## Mean p on logit scale logit.p.var <- 1 ## SD of p on logit scale p.h <- plogis(rnorm(N, logit.p.bar, logit.p.var)) ``` ::: All capture histories (for captured and uncaptured individuals) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.all.Mh <- matrix(NA, N, J) for(i in 1:N) { y.all.Mh[i,] <- rbinom(J, 1, p.h[i]) } ``` ::: Observed capture histories (data) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} captured.Mh <- rowSums(y.all.Mh)>0 n.Mh <- sum(captured.Mh) y.Mh <- y.all.Mh[captured.Mh,] #y.Mh[1:3,] ``` ::: ::: # Joint likelihood ## R package `RMark' ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Before you can use 'RMark', you have to install MARK.
The main MARK page is [here]( http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/index.html).
[Instructions for Linux and Mac users](http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/rmark/linux/)
[Heather Gaya's tutorial](https://github.com/heathergaya/JAGS-NIMBLE-Tutorials/blob/master/Installing\%20RMark\%20on\%20Mac\%202022)
Lots of [good information about closed population mark-recapture](http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/docs/book/pdf/chap14.pdf) ::: ## R package 'RMark' -- Model *M~0~* ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Fit the model and set capture probability equal to recapture probability ($p=c$) using the `share` argument. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## install.packages("RMark") ## Must install MARK too!! library(RMark) y.ch <- data.frame(ch=apply(y, 1, paste, collapse="")) mark.M0 <- mark(data=y.ch, model="Closed", silent=TRUE, model.parameters=list(p=list(formula=~1,share=TRUE))) ``` ::: Estimates of $p$ and $n_0$ (called $f_0$ in MARK) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.M0$results$real ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate se lcl ucl fixed note p g1 t1 0.1837077 0.0374009 0.1212906 0.2684329 f0 g1 a0 t1 42.6208640 16.7216950 20.3019990 89.4758200 ``` ::: ::: Estimate of $N$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.M0$results$derived ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $`N Population Size` estimate se lcl ucl 1 96.62086 16.7217 74.302 143.4758 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## R package `RMark' -- Model *M~t~* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yt.ch <- data.frame(ch=apply(y.Mt, 1, paste, collapse="")) mark.Mt <- mark(data=yt.ch, model="Closed", silent=TRUE, model.parameters=list(p=list(formula=~time,share=TRUE))) ``` ::: Estimates of $p_j$ and $n_0$ (called $f_0$ in MARK) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.Mt$results$real ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate se lcl ucl fixed note p g1 t1 0.2740198 0.0473865 0.1913594 0.3757930 p g1 t2 0.5186804 0.0592722 0.4035760 0.6318356 p g1 t3 0.2153013 0.0428690 0.1429996 0.3108977 p g1 t4 0.3718840 0.0532543 0.2746824 0.4806868 f0 g1 a0 t1 17.1823890 6.4441809 8.4388334 34.9852260 ``` ::: ::: Estimate of $N$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.Mt$results$derived ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $`N Population Size` estimate se lcl ucl 1 102.1824 6.444181 93.43883 119.9852 ``` ::: ::: ## R package `RMark' -- Model *M~b~* ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yb.ch <- data.frame(ch=apply(y.Mb, 1, paste, collapse="")) mark.Mb <- mark(data=yb.ch, model="Closed", silent=TRUE) ## Default model ``` ::: Estimates of $p$, $c$, and $n_0$ (called $f_0$ in MARK) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.Mb$results$real ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate se lcl ucl fixed note p g1 t1 0.2459652 0.0827673 0.1197363 0.4389147 c g1 t2 0.4031008 0.0431879 0.3220497 0.4898126 f0 g1 a0 t1 33.4146850 23.1165880 9.8085806 113.8331000 ``` ::: ::: Estimate of $N$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.Mb$results$derived ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $`N Population Size` estimate se lcl ucl 1 104.4147 23.11659 80.80858 184.8331 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## 'RMark' -- Model *M~h~* ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} This is a two-point mixture model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yh.ch <- data.frame(ch=apply(y.Mh.mix, 1, paste, collapse="")) mark.Mh <- mark(data=yh.ch, silent=TRUE, model="HetClosed", # "HugHet", model.parameters=list(p=list(formula=~mixture,share=TRUE))) ``` ::: Estimates of $p$ and $\pi$, the proportion of individuals in group 2. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.Mh$results$real ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` estimate se lcl ucl fixed note pi g1 m1 0.6554419 0.1938704 0.2612437 0.9109758 p g1 t1 m1 0.3985716 0.1171103 0.2027864 0.6332369 p g1 t1 m2 0.8435083 0.1105444 0.5107922 0.9653087 f0 g1 a0 t1 7.6766948 5.7418263 2.0786066 28.3515140 ``` ::: ::: Estimate of $N$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mark.Mh$results$derived ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $`N Population Size` estimate se lcl ucl 1 94.67669 5.741826 89.07861 115.3515 ``` ::: ::: ::: # Data augmentation ## Data augmentation ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} Data augmentation is strange.
We add "all zero" capture histories to our data, then we try to estimate how many of them are real.
::: {.fragment} The total number of observed and augmented encounter histories is $M$. We define the model in terms of a binary indicator variable $z_i$, such that $N=\sum_{i=1}^M z_i$.
We know $z_i=1$ for the $n$ captured individuals. ::: ::: ## Data augmentation ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} We can think about the problem like this: :::
::: {style='font-size: 45%;'} Individual | 1 | 2 | 3 | z --------- | ----- | ------ | ----- | ----- 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 3 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 4 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 5 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | 1 $n$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 $n+1$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | ? $n+2$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | ? $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | ? $N$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | ? $N+1$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | ? $N+2$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | ? $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | ? $M$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | ? :::
## Data augmentation ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} The model: $$ z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi) \\ y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_i \times p_{ij}) \\ N=\sum_{i=1}^M z_i $$ Note that this looks exactly like an occupancy model. ::: {.fragment} But why bother with augmentation? - DA works for *all* varieties of mark-recapture models - Makes it easy to incorporate individual-covariates... including distance and location. ::: ::: ## Data augmentation ::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} First, let's augment the data simulated under model $M_b$, with $M=200$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} M <- 200 y.aug <- matrix(0, M, J) y.aug[1:nrow(y.Mb),] <- y.Mb ``` :::
We also need to augment the `prevcap` object. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prevcap.aug <- matrix(FALSE, M, J) prevcap.aug[1:nrow(y.Mb),] <- prevcap[captured.Mb,] prevcap.aug <- ifelse(prevcap.aug, "Yes", "No") ``` ::: ::: ## Bayesian data augmentation ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} For Bayesian inference, we need priors on $\psi$ and $p$. $$ z_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi) \\ y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_i \times p) \\ N = \sum_{i=1}^M z_i $$
::: {.fragment} A uniform prior on $\psi$ results in a discrete uniform prior on $N$. We can change the prior for $N$ by changing the prior on $\psi$, recognizing: $$ E(N)=M\psi $$ ::: ::: ## Model *M~0~* -- data augmentation [M0-aug.jag](M0-aug.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { p ~ dunif(0,1) ## Capture probability psi ~ dunif(0,1) ## Data augmentation parameter for(i in 1:M) { z[i] ~ dbern(psi) ## DA indicator for(j in 1:J) { y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i]*p) ## Model for the capture histories } } N <- sum(z) ## Abundance } ``` ::: ::: ## Model *M~0~* -- data augmentation Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y.aug <- matrix(0, M, J) y.aug[1:n,] <- y jags.data.M0 <- list(y=y.aug, M=M, J=J) ``` ::: Inits and parameters ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ji.M0 <- function() list(z=rep(1,M), psi=runif(1), p=runif(1)) jp.M0 <- c("p", "psi", "N") ``` ::: MCMC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(jagsUI) jags.post.M0 <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.M0, inits=ji.M0, parameters.to.save=jp.M0, model.file="M0-aug.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-cap-recap-nonspatial_files/figure-revealjs/plot-mcmc-M0-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Model *M~b~* -- data augmentation [Mb-aug.jag](Mb-aug.jag) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { p ~ dunif(0, 1) ## Capture prob c ~ dunif(0, 1) ## Recapture prob psi ~ dunif(0,1) ## Data augmentation parameter for(i in 1:M) { z[i] ~ dbern(psi) ## DA indicator for(j in 1:J) { pc[i,j] <- ifelse(prevcap[i,j]==0, p, c) ## First cap or recap? y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i]*pc[i,j]) } } N <- sum(z) } ``` ::: ::: ## Model *M~b~* -- data augmentation Data, inits, parameters to monitor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.data.Mb <- jags.data.M0 jags.data.Mb$y[1:nrow(y.Mb),] <- y.Mb jags.data.Mb$prevcap <- ifelse(prevcap.aug=="Yes", 1, 0) ji.Mb <- function() list(z=rep(1,M), psi=runif(1), p=runif(1), c=runif(1)) jp.Mb <- c("p", "c", "psi", "N") ``` ::: MCMC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} jags.post.Mb <- jags.basic(data=jags.data.Mb, inits=ji.Mb, parameters.to.save=jp.Mb, model.file="Mb-aug.jag", n.chains=3, n.adapt=100, n.burnin=0, n.iter=2000, parallel=TRUE) ``` ::: ## Traceplots and density plots ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-cap-recap-nonspatial_files/figure-revealjs/plot-mcmc-Mb-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Model *M~h~* -- finite mixture ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { p1 ~ dunif(0, 1) ## Capture prob, group 1 p2 ~ dunif(0, 1) ## Capture prob, group 2 mixprob ~ dunif(0,1) ## Finite mixture prob psi ~ dunif(0,1) ## Data augmentation parameter for(i in 1:M) { z[i] ~ dbern(psi) ## DA indicator group[i] ~ dbern(mixprob) ## Group 1 or 2? p[i] <- ifelse(group[i]==0, p1, p2) ## p depends on group for(j in 1:J) { y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i]*p[i]) } } N <- sum(z) } ``` ::: ::: ## Model *M~h~* -- logit normal ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model { lp.mean ~ dnorm(0,0.1) ## Mean of logit(p) lp.var ~ dexp(1) ## Variance of logit(p) psi ~ dunif(0,1) ## Data augmentation parameter for(i in 1:M) { z[i] ~ dbern(psi) ## DA indicator lp[i] ~ dnorm(lp.mean, 1/lp.var) ## Random effect, p on logit p[i] <- ilogit(lp[i]) ## Capture prob for individual i for(j in 1:J) { y[i,j] ~ dbern(z[i]*p[i]) } } N <- sum(z) } ``` ::: ::: ## Mark-recapture summary ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} We assume that variation in $p$ arises from changes over time, behavioral effects, or random individual heterogeneity.
::: {.fragment} Individual heterogeneity models pose estimation problems. :::
::: {.fragment} A solution is to use individual covariates to explain the variation, rather than random effects. But what covariates are important? And how do we know the covariates values for uncaptured individuals? :::
::: {.fragment} With spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models we will use *the unobserved distance between animals and traps* as a covariate, and we'll use a spatial point process model for animal locations. ::: ::: # Assignment ## Assignment ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Create a self-contained R script or Rmarkdown file to do the following: - Import the Canada warbler mark-recapture data `CAWAcaps_2018.csv` and fit the following models in RMark and JAGS^[For JAGS, use $M=800$ but note if the posterior of $N$ pushes up against $M$.]: * Model $M_0$ * Model $M_t$ * Model $M_h$ -- Finite mixture * Model $M_h$ -- Logit-normal (JAGS only) - Create a table reporting point estimates and 95% CIs for $N$ for each model fit in RMark and JAGS. Which model has the lowest AICc (RMark only)?
Upload your `.R` or `.Rmd` file to ELC by 5:00pm on Tuesday.
:::
